title: Kotter Step 7 — Sustain Acceleration

sources.title: Leading Change
sources.reference: Kotter, J. P. (1996). Leading Change. Harvard Business Review Press.

terminal_objective: Explain what it means to sustain acceleration (Step 7), and describe why change efforts commonly stall at this stage.
performance_context: When observing a change effort that has produced early wins, the learner should be able to recognize the specific risks of the post-win phase and distinguish sustained acceleration from either premature declaration of victory or exhausting continued effort.

enabling_objective.statement: Describe what sustaining acceleration means after short-term wins, and explain the two main patterns that cause change efforts to stall at this stage.

concepts.name: Sustaining acceleration
concepts.definition: Using the credibility generated by short-term wins to pursue more ambitious change, rather than treating the wins as evidence that the effort is complete. Sustaining acceleration means pressing the advantage, not maintaining it.
concepts.elaboration: The word 'acceleration' is deliberate. Kotter does not describe Step 7 as 'sustain progress' or 'maintain momentum' — he describes it as sustaining acceleration, meaning the change effort should move faster after early wins, not slower. The wins provide the credibility and organizational learning needed to take on harder work; scaling back at this point squanders that credibility.

misconceptions.statement: After early wins, the change should be scaled back and consolidated before further effort.
misconceptions.correction: Kotter argues the opposite. Early wins produce the credibility, organizational learning, and reduced resistance that make more ambitious change possible. Scaling back after early wins wastes that opportunity and is a common failure mode. Step 7 is 'sustain acceleration,' not 'sustain steady state.'

misconceptions.statement: Sustaining acceleration means continuing to do the same things that produced the early wins.
misconceptions.correction: Early wins typically come from pilots or focused initiatives with favorable conditions. Sustaining acceleration means expanding to harder cases — scaling to less favorable regions, deeper structural changes, or more ambitious initiatives. Simply repeating what worked in the pilot does not produce the same results at scale.

concepts.name: Common stalling patterns
concepts.definition: Change efforts most often stall at Step 7 through two specific patterns: premature victory declaration (treating early wins as the end) and change fatigue (attempting to sustain effort without escalating scope, exhausting the organization).
concepts.elaboration: Premature victory declaration is externally driven — stakeholders, media, or leadership itself celebrate the early wins and lose interest in continued investment. Change fatigue is internally driven — the coalition and volunteer army continue working at the same intensity on the same scope, and eventually burn out without a clear signal that harder, more ambitious work is next. Both patterns look different but produce the same outcome: the effort stalls before Step 8 is possible.

misconceptions.statement: If the coalition maintains its intensity, the change will succeed.
misconceptions.correction: Maintained intensity without escalating scope produces change fatigue. The organization needs signals that the effort is moving toward something harder and more valuable, not that it will simply continue at current intensity indefinitely. Kotter's model requires escalation, not sustained repetition.

misconceptions.statement: Stakeholders who celebrate early wins are supporting the effort.
misconceptions.correction: Celebration is not support if it comes with reduced investment or the expectation that the work is done. Coalition leaders must actively counter the 'we won' narrative that emerges after early wins, or the effort will be starved of resources before Step 8. Celebration must be paired with clear communication that the harder work is still ahead.

components.canonical_content: Step 7 is where a shocking number of change efforts fail — not because anything went wrong, but because things went right and everyone concluded the work was done. Kotter identifies this as one of the most common patterns in change failure: an organization produces its Step 6 wins, celebrates, quietly scales back the effort, and watches the change revert over the following year. Understanding what to do after the early wins is the difference between a change that endures and one that briefly happens.

Sustaining acceleration means using the credibility from short-term wins to pursue harder and more ambitious change — not treating the wins as an endpoint. The word 'acceleration' is deliberate: the effort should move faster after early wins, not slower or steady.

Change efforts stall at Step 7 through two main patterns. Premature victory declaration: stakeholders and leadership treat early wins as the end and reduce investment. Change fatigue: the coalition maintains intensity without escalating scope, exhausting the organization. Both patterns are common and both must be actively countered by the coalition.

components.title: Using early wins to enable harder work

canonical_content.setup: A retailer's change effort has produced three pilot-region wins at month 12. Rather than declare victory, the coalition uses the wins to justify tackling the two hardest regions — where union relationships and legacy operating models had made earlier attempts politically infeasible.
canonical_content.what_happens: The wins have shifted the political ground. Skeptics in the harder regions have less credibility with which to resist; volunteers in those regions can point to the pilot successes as evidence. The coalition takes on work at month 12 that would have been impossible at month 6.
canonical_content.reasoning: This is what sustained acceleration looks like. The early wins are treated as fuel for the harder work, not as evidence that work is done. Notice the escalation: harder regions, deeper change, more ambitious scope.

components.title: The coalition that expands the effort

canonical_content.setup: A financial services firm's change effort produces its Step 6 wins at month 15. The coalition, anticipating the 'we won' narrative, deliberately expands the effort: adding two new initiatives to the strategic portfolio, increasing volunteer army enrollment, and communicating explicitly that the wins are milestones on a longer path.
canonical_content.what_happens: The narrative around the effort remains one of ambition rather than completion. Stakeholders continue to invest; volunteers do not disengage; the coalition does not lose political capital. By month 24, the effort has produced deeper changes than would have been possible if it had defended its early wins.
canonical_content.reasoning: The coalition here is actively countering the premature-victory pattern. This is not passive continuation — it is a deliberate reframing of the wins as the beginning of the harder work, not the achievement of the goal.

canonical_content.setup: A change effort produces strong early wins at month 12. The CEO features the effort in the annual report as a completed transformation. Investment is reduced; the coalition is thanked and partially dispersed to new priorities.
canonical_content.why_wrong: The wins were Step 6, not Step 8. Institution of change (Step 8) had not occurred — the new behaviors were not yet embedded in the culture, and without sustained pressure they were still reversible. Within 18 months of the celebration, the organization had drifted back toward its pre-change operating model. The wins were real, but they did not survive the withdrawal of sustained effort.
canonical_content.correct_framing: Coalition leaders must actively counter the 'transformation complete' narrative. Celebration is appropriate; reduced investment is not. The next 12 months after Step 6 wins are typically when the most consequential work happens — not the least.

canonical_content.setup: A coalition twelve months into a change effort continues to work at high intensity on the same set of initiatives that produced the early wins. Volunteers are asked to maintain their engagement; managers are asked to keep pushing the same behaviors. No new scope is added.
canonical_content.why_wrong: The organization sees no signal that the effort is moving toward something harder or more valuable. The intensity that made sense at month 6 begins to feel exhausting and pointless at month 18 without a clear escalation. Volunteers disengage, coalition members burn out, and the effort stalls not from external opposition but from internal exhaustion.
canonical_content.correct_framing: Sustained acceleration requires escalating scope, not just maintained intensity. The organization needs to see that the effort is going somewhere new, not just continuing to do the same things at the same pitch.

canonical_content.prompt: In one sentence: what does 'sustain acceleration' mean in Kotter's model, and what are the two main patterns that cause change efforts to stall at this stage?
canonical_content.expected_answer: Sustaining acceleration means using the credibility from short-term wins to pursue harder and more ambitious change; the two main stalling patterns are premature victory declaration (external stakeholders treat early wins as the end) and change fatigue (the coalition maintains intensity without escalating scope).

assessment_items.stem: A change effort has produced strong Step 6 wins. Executive stakeholders congratulate the team, media coverage describes the transformation as 'successful,' and there are discussions about reducing the coalition's dedicated resources so team members can return to their regular roles. How should the coalition respond?

options.text: Accept the reduced resources and consolidate the wins already achieved.
options.feedback: This is premature victory declaration — precisely the pattern Step 7 exists to counter. The wins are Step 6 milestones, not Step 8 completion. Accepting reduced resources at this point virtually guarantees the change will revert over the following 12-24 months as sustained pressure is withdrawn.

options.text: Actively counter the 'transformation complete' narrative and use the wins to justify expanded ambition — harder cases, deeper changes, more visible initiatives.
options.feedback: Correct. This is sustained acceleration. The wins provide credibility that makes harder work politically possible; using them to defend existing progress rather than pursue new ambition wastes the opportunity. The coalition's job at this moment is to reframe the wins as milestones, not endpoints.

options.text: Continue the same set of initiatives at the same intensity, maintaining what is working.
options.feedback: Maintained intensity without escalating scope produces change fatigue. The organization needs signals that the effort is moving toward harder and more valuable work, not that it will simply continue at current pitch. Repetition of what worked in pilots does not produce Step 8 outcomes.

options.text: Declare the effort complete and shift focus to the next strategic initiative.
options.feedback: This is the most extreme form of premature victory declaration. The change has not been instituted — the wins demonstrate feasibility, not permanence. Declaring completion at this point and moving on virtually guarantees the change will revert.

assessment_items.stem: Eighteen months into a change effort, the coalition observes that volunteer engagement is declining and coalition members are showing signs of burnout. The initiatives are the same ones that produced Step 6 wins at month 12; the intensity of work has been maintained; but the organization feels tired. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The coalition has been over-resourced and needs to scale back the effort.
options.feedback: Scaling back after Step 6 wins is premature victory declaration in disguise. The problem described is not too much effort — it is effort without escalation of scope. Scaling back would compound the failure rather than address it.

options.text: Change fatigue — the coalition maintained intensity without escalating scope, so the organization has no signal that the effort is moving toward something new.
options.feedback: Correct. This is the classic change fatigue pattern. Maintained intensity on the same scope loses meaning over time — the organization needs to see that the effort is going somewhere. The fix is not to reduce effort but to escalate scope: add ambitious new initiatives, expand to harder cases, signal that the effort is on the way to Step 8, not stuck in an extended Step 6.

options.text: The change effort was insufficiently ambitious from the start.
options.feedback: The stem does not describe an insufficient starting ambition — it describes an effort that produced Step 6 wins at month 12 and then failed to escalate. The problem is the missing escalation at month 12, not the original scope.

options.text: The coalition should push harder to overcome the burnout.
options.feedback: Pushing harder at the same scope will accelerate burnout, not resolve it. The organization is not tired because it is doing too much; it is tired because it is doing the same things without a signal of progress toward something more ambitious. Escalation of scope, not intensity, is the correct response.

design_brief.tone: Cautionary and precise. This RLO is teaching learners to recognize a counterintuitive failure pattern — success that leads to failure. The tone should support the learner's ability to hold that tension without dismissing it.
design_brief.scaffolding_notes: Learners have completed RLOs 01, 02, and 08. The connection to Step 6 wins is essential — Step 7 is specifically about what to do with those wins, and the failure modes are both variants of mishandling them.
design_brief.feedback_policy: Feedback must distinguish clearly between the two stalling patterns (premature victory and change fatigue). They produce similar outcomes (stalled effort) but require opposite responses (more escalation vs. escalation with reduced repetition). Conflating them produces the wrong fix.
example_shape_hints: Include at least one example of successful sustained acceleration (using wins to enable harder work) and non-examples of each of the two stalling patterns.
The 'expand rather than defend' framing is high-value and should be surfaced explicitly.
Non-examples should show the specific mechanism of failure, not just the outcome — learners need to see how the failure unfolds to recognize it in progress.
practice_shape_hints: Practice items should present a post-Step-6 scenario and ask the learner to diagnose whether the risk is premature victory or change fatigue.
At least one item should test the 'push harder' misconception, since it is the intuitive-but-wrong response to change fatigue.
design_brief.salience_hook_description: The hook should establish that Step 7 is where success can produce failure. Learners should leave believing that early wins are the beginning of the harder work, not the end of the effort.

gagne_event_mapping.event_3_stimulate_recall: Reference to RLO-08: the Step 6 wins are the input to Step 7. What the coalition does with those wins determines whether Step 8 is reachable.
gagne_event_mapping.event_7_provide_feedback: See feedback fields on each assessment_item option
gagne_event_mapping.event_9_enhance_retention: Handled at learning-path level; RLO-12 revisits Step 7 stalling as one of the most common skipped-step failures.

content_type_recommendations.rationale: The two failure patterns unfold over time in ways that benefit from narrative treatment. A case study format that traces the effort from Step 6 wins through Step 7 outcomes is well-suited.
A short video comparing three trajectories from the same Step 6 moment — sustained acceleration, premature victory, change fatigue — makes the differential diagnosis vivid.
The two-pattern framework is compact enough to render in text with scenarios.

authoring_rationale: Step 7 is where the model earns most of its keep — it is the specific late-stage failure Kotter's original research identified as most common. The two-pattern framework (premature victory / change fatigue) is the specific instructional payload. The emphasis on escalation of scope (rather than escalation of intensity) is included because it is counterintuitive to learners who default to 'work harder' as the response to fatigue. The connection to Step 8 is foreshadowed — sustained acceleration is what makes institution of change possible.
